claim: Two monkeys (Cebus apella) were trained to perform two sequential reaching tasks.
source: We trained two monkeys (Cebus apella) to perform two sequential reaching tasks.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and subjects used in the study.

claim: In one task, sequential movements were instructed by visual cues.
source: In one task, sequential movements were instructed by visual cues, whereas in the other task, movements were generated from memory after extended practice.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: In the other task, movements were generated from memory after extended practice.
source: In one task, sequential movements were instructed by visual cues, whereas in the other task, movements were generated from memory after extended practice.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: Injection of anisomycin in M1 had a marked effect on the performance of sequential movements that were guided by memory.
source: Injection of anisomycin in M1 had a marked effect on the performance of sequential movements that were guided by memory.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The anisomycin injection did not have a significant effect on the performance of movements guided by vision.
source: In contrast, the anisomycin injection did not have a significant effect on the performance of movements guided by vision.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: M1 of non-human primates is involved in the maintenance of skilled sequential movements.
source: These results suggest that M1 of non-human primates is involved in the maintenance of skilled sequential movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: The preparation for and generation of sequential movements is classically thought to depend on the supplementary motor area (SMA) and the pre-SMA.
source: The preparation for and generation of sequential movements is classically thought to depend on the supplementary motor area (SMA) and the pre-SMA (Roland et al., 1980; Tanji and Shima, 1994; Gerloff et al., 1997; Shima and Tanji, 1998; Nakamura et al., 1998; Nakamura et al., 1999; Hikosaka et al., 2002; Picard and Strick, 2001; Dayan and Cohen, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The primary motor cortex (M1) is thought to produce the patterns of muscle activity that are necessary to implement the motor plans generated by the premotor areas.
source: According to this view, the primary motor cortex (M1) is thought to produce the patterns of muscle activity that are necessary to implement the motor plans generated by the premotor areas.
evidence: This describes the classical view of M1 function based on established scientific understanding.

claim: M1 of humans and non-human primates is involved in the acquisition and maintenance of sequential movements.
source: There is growing evidence, however, that M1 of humans and non-human primates is involved in the acquisition and maintenance of sequential movements.
evidence: This statement summarizes evidence from multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The activity of some M1 neurons appears to reflect the serial order of potential target stimuli.
source: For example, the activity of some M1 neurons appears to reflect the serial order of potential target stimuli (Pellizzer et al., 1995; Carpenter et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A large number of M1 neurons (~40%) and metabolic activity reflected aspects of learned movement sequences.
source: Similarly, a large number of M1 neurons (~40%) and metabolic activity reflected aspects of learned movement sequences (Lu and Ashe, 2005; Matsuzaka et al., 2007; Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The functional connectivity of M1 neurons was suggested to be associated with sequential planning of movements.
source: In addition, the functional connectivity of M1 neurons was suggested to be associated with sequential planning of movements (Hatsopoulos et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: M1 is critical for implementing motor output.
source: M1 is critical for implementing motor output.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about M1 function.

claim: Lesion or inactivation of M1 will abolish the motor commands to the spinal cord that generate muscle activity.
source: Lesion or inactivation of M1 will abolish the motor commands to the spinal cord that generate muscle activity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about M1 function.

claim: Local injection of an inhibitor for protein synthesis, anisomycin, was shown to interfere with learning and maintenance of memory.
source: In these studies, local injection of an inhibitor for protein synthesis, anisomycin, was shown to interfere with learning and maintenance of memory (Davis and Squire, 1984; Nader et al., 2000a; Nader et al., 2000b; Kandel, 2001; Kleim et al., 2003; Dudai, 2004a; Luft et al., 2004; Dudai, 2012; Rudy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The monkeys practiced each sequence for more than 100 training days.
source: After the monkeys practiced each sequence for more than 100 training days and became proficient with performing the two tasks, we made injections of the protein synthesis inhibitor, anisomycin, in M1 to test M1's involvement in maintenance of sequential movements after the extensive practice.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: The injections of anisomycin solution (100 mg/ml) were placed at sites in which intracortical stimulation evoked shoulder or elbow movements.
source: The injections of aniomycin solution (100 mg/ml) were placed at sites in which intracortical stimulation evoked shoulder or elbow movements (Figure 1c–f, for details see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and is supported by figure references.

claim: The anisomycin injections had a significant effect on the performance of the movements during the Repeating task.
source: The anisomycin injections had a significant effect on the performance of the movements during the Repeating task (Figures 2 and 3a,b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The injections resulted in a significant increase in the number of errors during the Repeating task.
source: The injections resulted in a significant increase in the number of errors (Figures 2 and 3; χ2 test, p<0.05) and a significant decrease in the number of predictive responses, an indication of sequence learning, (Figure 3c; χ2 test, p<0.05) during the Repeating task.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: The injections resulted in a significant decrease in the number of predictive responses during the Repeating task.
source: The injections resulted in a significant increase in the number of errors (Figures 2 and 3; χ2 test, p<0.05) and a significant decrease in the number of predictive responses, an indication of sequence learning, (Figure 3c; χ2 test, p<0.05) during the Repeating task.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Predictive responses are an indication of sequence learning.
source: The injections resulted in a significant increase in the number of errors (Figures 2 and 3; χ2 test, p<0.05) and a significant decrease in the number of predictive responses, an indication of sequence learning, (Figure 3c; χ2 test, p<0.05) during the Repeating task.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental design and established understanding of motor learning.

claim: Performance of visually guided movements during the Random task was not significantly disrupted by anisomycin injection.
source: In contrast, performance of visually guided movements during the Random task was not significantly disrupted (χ2 test, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Anisomycin injection did not have any effect on number of errors during the Random task for movement 3-1.
source: Anisomycin injection did not have any effect on number of errors during the Random task (χ2 test, p=0.385 for move 3–1, df = 1; p=0.639 for move 5–3, df = 1; p=0.624 for move 1–5, df = 1; not significant for move 4–1, df = 1; p=0.957 for move 1–2, df = 1; p=0.371 for move 2–4, df = 1).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: After the anisomycin injection, the number of errors increased dramatically in 5 of 6 movements in the Repeating task.
source: After the anisomycin injection, the number of errors increased dramatically in 5 of 6 movements in the Repeating task (χ2 test, p<0.001 for moves 5–3, 1–5, 4–1 and 2–4, df = 1; p=0.689 for move 3–1, df = 1; p=0.004 for move 1–2, df = 1).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of predictive responses decreased significantly after the anisomycin injection for all movements in the Repeating task.
source: The percentage of predictive responses decreased significantly after the anisomycin injection (χ2 test, p<0.001 for all movements, df = 1).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Before the injection, the monkey made correct contact to target 5 on 96% of the trials in the Repeating task (sequence 5-3-1).
source: As shown in Figure 2a, before the injection, the monkey made correct contact to target 5 on 96% of the trials in the Repeating task (sequence 5-3-1).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experiment shown in a figure.

claim: After the anisomycin injection, the monkey made accuracy errors on 45% of the trials for movement 1-5.
source: After the anisomycin injection, the number of incorrect responses increased dramatically. The monkey then made accuracy errors on 45% of the trials (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experiment shown in a figure.

claim: The monkey made a correct movement to target 4 on 93% of the trials in the Repeating task (sequence 1-2-4) before the injection.
source: As shown in Figure 2b, the monkey made a correct movement to target 4 on 93% of the trials in the Repeating task (sequence 1-2-4) before the injection.
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experiment shown in a figure.

claim: After the anisomycin injection, the animal made direction errors on 18% of the trials in the Repeating task for movement 2-4.
source: After the anisomycin injection, the animal moved his arm to the left from target 2 and made direction errors on 18% of the trials in the Repeating task (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experiment shown in a figure.

claim: Direction errors suggest a deficit in selecting the movement component in the sequence.
source: This type of error suggests a deficit in selecting the movement component in the sequence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed error patterns.

claim: For the injection session illustrated in Figures 2 and 3, the error rate increased significantly for five of the six movements performed during the Repeating task.
source: For the injection session illustrated in Figures 2 and 3, the error rate increased significantly for five of the six movements performed during the Repeating task.
evidence: This is a summary of data shown in the figures.

claim: A significant increase in error rate during the Repeating task was observed for all of six injection sessions.
source: Overall, we observed a significant increase in error rate during the Repeating task for all of six injection sessions (χ2 test, p<0.05; monkey N, n = 4; monkey R, n = 2).
evidence: This is a summary finding across all experimental sessions with statistical support.

claim: The effect of anisomycin was more pronounced for certain moves of the learned sequences.
source: The effect of anisomycin was more pronounced for certain moves of the learned sequences (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The affected moves varied between sessions.
source: The affected moves varied between sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data across sessions.

claim: The error rate increased by an average of 42% for the most affected movements during the Repeating task.
source: The error rate increased by an average of 42% for the most affected movements during the Repeating task (Figure 4b; paired t-test; p=0.002).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: The effect of anisomycin injections were consistent between monkeys.
source: The effect of anisomycin injections were consistent between monkeys (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary observation supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The performance changes observed in the Repeating task are attributed to the effect of anisomycin injection on memory.
source: Given that performance of the Random task was unaffected, we attribute the performance changes observed in the Repeating task to the effect of anisomycin injection on memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects observed between the two tasks.

claim: The effect of injections on the error rates was strong and consistent for the Repeating task and was consistently nonexistent for the Random task.
source: Overall, the effect of injections on the error rates was strong and consistent for the Repeating task and was consistently nonexistent for the Random task.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings across all sessions.

claim: The ratio of predictive trials decreased from 92.4% to 35.3% for the most affected movement (target 5 to 3) during the Repeating task.
source: As shown in Figure 3c, the ratio of predictive trials decreased from 92.4% to 35.3% for the most affected movement, from target 5 to 3, during the Repeating task (χ2 test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of predictive movements during the Repeating task was observed for all of six injection sessions.
source: Overall, we observed a significant decrease in the number of predictive movements during the Repeating task for all of six injection sessions (χ2 test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a summary finding across all experimental sessions with statistical support.

claim: The ratio of predictive responses decreased by an average of 55.7% for the most affected movements during the Repeating task.
source: The ratio of predictive responses decreased by an average of 55.7% for the most affected movements during the Repeating task (Figure 4c; paired t-test, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: A decrease in the number of predictive responses suggests an increase in the time for movement selection.
source: A decrease in the number of predictive responses suggests an increase in the time for movement selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed changes in predictive responses.

claim: In the non-predictive trials, it is possible that the monkey used the visual cue information to make a correct response since the animal's performance in the Random task was not affected by the injections.
source: In the non-predictive trials, it is possible that the monkey used the visual cue information to make a correct response since the animal's performance in the Random task was not affected by the injections.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: After the injections, during the Repeating task, MTs significantly increased in 73.3% of the movements.
source: After the injections, during the Repeating task, MTs significantly increased in 73.3% of the movements and RTs significantly increased for all the movements (two monkeys, six injections, t-test, p<0.05; averaged increase of MT: 45.82 msec, averaged increase of RT: 140.23 msec).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: After the injections, during the Repeating task, RTs significantly increased for all the movements.
source: After the injections, during the Repeating task, MTs significantly increased in 73.3% of the movements and RTs significantly increased for all the movements (two monkeys, six injections, t-test, p<0.05; averaged increase of MT: 45.82 msec, averaged increase of RT: 140.23 msec).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The averaged increase of MT during the Repeating task was 45.82 msec.
source: After the injections, during the Repeating task, MTs significantly increased in 73.3% of the movements and RTs significantly increased for all the movements (two monkeys, six injections, t-test, p<0.05; averaged increase of MT: 45.82 msec, averaged increase of RT: 140.23 msec).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The averaged increase of RT during the Repeating task was 140.23 msec.
source: After the injections, during the Repeating task, MTs significantly increased in 73.3% of the movements and RTs significantly increased for all the movements (two monkeys, six injections, t-test, p<0.05; averaged increase of MT: 45.82 msec, averaged increase of RT: 140.23 msec).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The increase of RT and MT may reflect the monkeys' hesitation, uncertainty about the next target or change of the strategy.
source: The increase of RT and MT may reflect the monkeys' hesitation, uncertainty about the next target or change of the strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed changes in timing measures.

claim: During the Random task, the injections did not cause a significant change in movement times for most of the movements in 5 of 6 injections.
source: On the other hand, during the Random task, the injections did not cause a significant change in movement times for most of the movements in 5 of 6 injections (t-test, p>0.05).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: During the Random task, RTs increased in sixty percent of the movements.
source: Overall, during the Random task, RTs increased in sixty percent of the movements (t-test, p<0.05, averaged increase of RT: 84.61 msec; averaged increase of MT: 38.73 msec).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The averaged increase of RT during the Random task was 84.61 msec.
source: Overall, during the Random task, RTs increased in sixty percent of the movements (t-test, p<0.05, averaged increase of RT: 84.61 msec; averaged increase of MT: 38.73 msec).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The averaged increase of MT during the Random task was 38.73 msec.
source: Overall, during the Random task, RTs increased in sixty percent of the movements (t-test, p<0.05, averaged increase of RT: 84.61 msec; averaged increase of MT: 38.73 msec).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The effects on RT and MT were strong and consistent within the Repeating task, but were weak and variable within the Random task.
source: In summary, the effects on RT and MT were strong and consistent within the Repeating task, but were weak and variable within the Random task.
evidence: This is a summary of the timing data across both tasks.

claim: Anisomycin injection in M1 impaired performance of the Repeating task for 1–2 days after the injection.
source: Anisomycin injection in M1 impaired performance of the Repeating task for 1–2 days after the injection (χ2 test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding about the temporal duration of the effect, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The task performance returned to the baseline after 1–2 days of training.
source: The task performance returned to the baseline after 1–2 days of training (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding about recovery of performance, supported by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: M1 inactivations by muscimol impaired performance on both the Random and Repeating tasks.
source: We found that M1 inactivations impaired performance on both the Random and Repeating tasks (χ2 test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments supported by statistical analysis.

claim: M1 inactivation caused an indiscriminate deficit of motor production.
source: The results indicate that M1 inactivation caused an indiscriminate deficit of motor production.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the muscimol control experiment results.

claim: Injection of saline into M1 did not have any significant effects on performance of both the Random and Repeating tasks.
source: Injection of saline into M1 did not have any significant effects on performance of both the Random and Repeating tasks (χ2 test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Localized inhibition of protein synthesis in M1 resulted in a selective deficit in the performance of internally generated sequential movements during the Repeating task.
source: In the present study, localized inhibition of protein synthesis in M1 resulted in a selective deficit in the performance of internally generated sequential movements during the Repeating task.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: This observation emphasizes the importance of M1 for the generation of sequential movements that are memory guided.
source: This observation emphasizes the importance of M1 for the generation of sequential movements that are memory guided.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: M1 is critical for movement production.
source: Our results suggest that, although M1 is critical for movement production, it also is involved in the maintenance of skilled sequential movements.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: M1 is involved in the maintenance of skilled sequential movements.
source: Our results suggest that, although M1 is critical for movement production, it also is involved in the maintenance of skilled sequential movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: M1 is reorganized after extensive practice of sequential movements.
source: Growing evidence showed that M1 is reorganized after extensive practice of sequential movements, yet our understanding of its neural basis after extensive practice is still limited.
evidence: This is a statement about existing evidence in the field.

claim: The volume of M1 is larger in professional musicians compared to amateurs or non-musicians.
source: Human imaging studies reported that the volume of M1 is larger in professional musicians compared to amateurs or non-musicians suggesting that there is an effect of extensive practice on M1 structure (Amunts et al., 1997; Gaser and Schlaug, 2003; Zatorre et al., 2012; Draganski and May, 2008; Herholz and Zatorre, 2012; Sampaio-Baptista and Johansen-Berg, 2017; Wenger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: There is an effect of extensive practice on M1 structure.
source: Human imaging studies reported that the volume of M1 is larger in professional musicians compared to amateurs or non-musicians suggesting that there is an effect of extensive practice on M1 structure (Amunts et al., 1997; Gaser and Schlaug, 2003; Zatorre et al., 2012; Draganski and May, 2008; Herholz and Zatorre, 2012; Sampaio-Baptista and Johansen-Berg, 2017; Wenger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from cited studies showing structural differences in musicians.

claim: After years of training, 40% of M1 neurons were differentially active during the performance of visually guided and memory guided sequential reaching.
source: After years of training, 40% of M1 neurons were differentially active during the performance of visually guided and memory guided sequential reaching (Matsuzaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Uptake of 2DG in arm M1 was shown to be low in monkeys that performed highly practiced, internally generated sequences of movements.
source: Uptake of 2DG in arm M1 was shown to be low in monkeys that performed highly practiced, internally generated sequences of movements (Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: M1 is involved in sequential movements after extensive practice.
source: Our current observations also suggest that M1 is involved in sequential movements after extensive practice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current study's results in the context of prior research.

claim: Injection of anisomycin into the motor cortex after 14 days of task training disrupted the performance of the skilled forelimb task in rats.
source: Kleim and his colleagues reported that an injection of anisomycin into the motor cortex after 14 days of the task training disrupted the performance of the skilled forelimb task (Kleim et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The injection of anisomycin not only disrupted the performance of the motor skill task, but also caused a significant reduction in synapse number and synapse size in M1 in vivo.
source: The injection of anisomycin not only disrupted the performance of the motor skill task, but also caused a significant reduction in synapse number and synapse size in M1 in vivo (Kleim et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Injection of anisomycin into the motor cortex after the 1st and 2nd days of training on the task disrupted the learning of the task in rats.
source: Luft and his colleagues reported that injection of anisomycin into the motor cortex after the 1st and 2nd days of training on the task disrupted the learning of the task (Luft et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The anisomycin injection interfered with the learning or maintenance of the forelimb motor skills such as reaching and grasping in rodents.
source: These studies suggested that the anisomycin injection interfered with the learning or maintenance of the forelimb motor skills such as reaching and grasping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of cited rodent studies.

claim: De novo protein synthesis, during or shortly after initial training, is shown to be an essential step in consolidation of long-term memory.
source: De novo protein synthesis, during or shortly after initial training, is shown to be an essential step in consolidation of long-term memory (Davis and Squire, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Studies using anisomycin suggested the neural trace of memory may become labile upon retrieval, after which it may be reconsolidated.
source: Moreover, the studies using anisomycin suggested the neural trace of memory may become labile upon retrieval, after which it may be reconsolidated (Nader et al., 2000a; reviewed in Dudai, 2012 and Rudy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neural trace may be destabilized through protein degradation and rebounded through protein synthesis during the reconsolidation.
source: These studies using anisomycin suggested that the neural trace may be destabilized through protein degradation and rebounded through protein synthesis during the reconsolidation (Nader et al., 2000a; Nader, 2003; Sara, 2000; Lee et al., 2008; Rudy, 2008; Rudy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The destabilized trace is proposed to be bi-directionally modified (i.e. weakened or strengthened), so that the memory can be 'updated'.
source: The destabilized trace is proposed to be bi-directionally modified (i.e. weakened or strengthened), so that the memory can be 'updated' (Rudy, 2008; Sara, 2000; Dudai, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When the protein synthesis inhibitor, anisomycin, was given during retrieval, the retrieved memory trace was lost as anisomycin prevents synthesis of the proteins needed to reconsolidate the memory trace.
source: Thus, when the protein synthesis inhibitor, anisomycin, was given during retrieval, the retrieved memory trace was lost as anisomycin prevents synthesis of the proteins needed to reconsolidate the memory trace (Nader et al., 2000a; Lee et al., 2008; Dudai, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neural traces for sequential movements may be repetitively strengthened over multiple sessions of practice through lingering protein synthesis in M1.
source: These observations suggest that the neural traces for sequential movements may be repetitively strengthened over multiple sessions of practice through lingering protein synthesis in M1, which may lead to an increase of synaptic efficacy in M1 and slow improvement of the task performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the current study's results.

claim: Repetitive strengthening of neural traces may lead to an increase of synaptic efficacy in M1 and slow improvement of the task performance.
source: These observations suggest that the neural traces for sequential movements may be repetitively strengthened over multiple sessions of practice through lingering protein synthesis in M1, which may lead to an increase of synaptic efficacy in M1 and slow improvement of the task performance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the current study's results.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for long-lasting synaptic plasticity (late long-term potentiation).
source: Furthermore, studies using brain slices showed that protein synthesis is required for long-lasting synaptic plasticity (late long-term potentiation) (reviewed in Kelleher et al., 2004) and spine-head enlargement and growth during learning (Steward and Levy, 1982; Steward and Fass, 1983; Steward and Schuman, 2003; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for spine-head enlargement and growth during learning.
source: Furthermore, studies using brain slices showed that protein synthesis is required for long-lasting synaptic plasticity (late long-term potentiation) (reviewed in Kelleher et al., 2004) and spine-head enlargement and growth during learning (Steward and Levy, 1982; Steward and Fass, 1983; Steward and Schuman, 2003; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The effects of protein synthesis inhibitors on long-lasting synaptic plasticity are likely to be a specific consequence of their translational blockade.
source: Several observations indicate that the effects of protein synthesis inhibitors on long-lasting synaptic plasticity are likely to be a specific consequence of their translational blockade (Linden, 1996; Huber et al., 2000; Beaumont et al., 2001; Kelleher et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies in rodents support the finding that inhibition of protein synthesis in M1 of monkeys interfered with performance of sequential movements guided by memory.
source: These studies in rodents support our finding that inhibition of protein synthesis in M1 of monkeys interfered with performance of sequential movements guided by memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting prior rodent studies to the current findings.

claim: M1 is densely interconnected with the dorsal premotor cortex proper (PMd).
source: M1 is densely interconnected with the dorsal premotor cortex proper (PMd) (Dum and Strick, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inactivation of the PMd resulted in a selective deficit in the performance of internally generated sequences.
source: We recently demonstrated that inactivation of the PMd resulted in a selective deficit in the performance of internally generated sequences (Ohbayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research by the same authors.

claim: The PMd contributes to the internal generation of sequential movements through maintaining motor-motor associations.
source: We proposed that the PMd contributes to the internal generation of sequential movements through maintaining motor-motor associations.
evidence: This is a proposal based on prior research by the same authors.

claim: The current results are consistent with the PMd functioning as a major source of input to M1 to guide the performance of internally generated sequences.
source: Our current results are consistent with the PMd functioning as a major source of input to M1 to guide the performance of internally generated sequences.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current results to prior findings about PMd.

claim: Extended practice on a sequence of movements resulted in dramatic alterations in the functional activation and neural responses of M1.
source: Previous studies reported that extended practice on a sequence of movements resulted in dramatic alterations in the functional activation and neural responses of M1 (Matsuzaka et al., 2007; Picard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human imaging studies found a functional and structural change in M1 of professional musicians.
source: In addition, human imaging studies found a functional and structural change in M1 of professional musicians (Elbert et al., 1995; Amunts et al., 1997; Gaser and Schlaug, 2003; Schwenkreis et al., 2007; Draganski and May, 2008; Herholz and Zatorre, 2012; Zatorre et al., 2012; Sampaio-Baptista and Johansen-Berg, 2017; Wenger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: M1's specific contribution to the acquisition and maintenance of sequential movements needs to be further explored in future experiments.
source: M1's specific contribution to the acquisition and maintenance of sequential movements needs to be further explored in future experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Two male Cebus apella monkeys weighing 3.2 kg and 3.7 kg were used in the study.
source: Two monkeys (Cebus apella, two males weighing 3.2 kg and 3.7 kg) were trained to perform two tasks, Random and Repeating tasks (Figure 1a,b) (Matsuzaka et al., 2007; Picard et al., 2013; Ohbayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: In the Random task, new targets were presented according to a pseudo-random order 100 ms after contact of the correct target.
source: In the Random task, new targets were presented according to a pseudo-random order 100 ms after contact of the correct target.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the Random task.

claim: In the Repeating task, new targets were presented according to a repeating sequence of three elements.
source: In the Repeating task, new targets were presented according to a repeating sequence of three elements.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the Repeating task.

claim: Three sequences were used in the experiments: 5-3-1-5-3-1 . . . and 1-2-4-1-2-4 . . . or 2-3-4-2-3-4 . . .
source: Three sequences were used in this experiments: 5-3-1-5-3-1 . . . and 1-2-4-1-2-4 . . . or 2-3-4-2-3-4 . . . (Figure 1a,b, two sequences for monkey N, one sequence for monkey R).
evidence: This describes the specific sequences used in the experimental protocol.

claim: In the Repeating task, new targets were presented 400 ms after contact of the correct target.
source: New targets were presented 400 ms after contact of the correct target. This 400 ms delay promoted the performance of predictive responses in which the animal anticipated the next target in a sequence.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for the Repeating task.

claim: The 400 ms delay promoted the performance of predictive responses in which the animal anticipated the next target in a sequence.
source: This 400 ms delay promoted the performance of predictive responses in which the animal anticipated the next target in a sequence.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the timing parameter in the experimental design.

claim: A liquid reward was given after every four to five correct responses.
source: A liquid reward was given after every four to five correct responses.
evidence: This describes the reward schedule used in the experimental protocol.

claim: The monkeys were introduced to the Repeating task after the monkeys became proficient in the performance of the Random task after about 50 days of practice.
source: The monkeys were introduced to the Repeating task after the monkeys became proficient in the performance of the Random task after about 50 days of practice.
evidence: This describes the training protocol used in the study.

claim: Both monkeys became proficient with performing the two tasks after more than 100 training sessions.
source: Both monkeys became proficient with performing the two tasks after more than 100 training sessions.
evidence: This describes the training duration before experimental manipulations.

claim: The injection experiments were performed after a monkey had more than 100 training sessions on each sequence.
source: The injection experiments were performed after a monkey had more than 100 training sessions on each sequence.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol timing.

claim: Intracortical microstimulation was used to identify the arm representation in M1 and to physiologically define the border between M1 and the PMd.
source: We used intracortical microstimulation to identify the arm representation in M1 and to physiologically define the border between M1 and the PMd (Dum and Strick, 2005; Ohbayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the method used to localize injection sites.

claim: For each injection session, a total of 5 or 10 μl anisomycin solution was injected into M1.
source: For each injection session, we injected total of 5 or 10 μl anisomycin solution into M1 (5 μl, n = 5; 10 μl, n = 1).
evidence: This describes the injection protocol used in the study.

claim: The anisomycin solution was injected at two to four sites in the arm representation area of M1.
source: To cover a large portion of the arm representation in M1, the anisomycin solution was injected at two to four sites in the arm representation area of M1 (Figures 1f, 1-3 μl at each site).
evidence: This describes the injection protocol used in the study.

claim: Injection sites were placed more than 2 mm away from the border between M1 and PMd identified by microstimulation.
source: Injection sites were placed more than 2 mm away from the border between M1 and PMd identified by microstimulation.
evidence: This describes the injection protocol used to ensure specificity to M1.

claim: Previous studies using monkeys reported that infusion of 3 µl of muscimol into cortex inhibited the activity of neurons within a diameter of 2–3 mm.
source: Previous studies using monkeys reported that infusion of 3 µl of muscimol into cortex inhibited the activity of neurons within a diameter of 2–3 mm (Nakamura et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The effect of 2–3 µl of a pharmacological agent was assumed to be limited to M1.
source: Therefore, the effect of 2–3 µl of a pharmacological agent was assumed to be limited to M1.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research about the spread of injected substances.

claim: The effect on performance of the tasks was tested 20–24 hr after the injection of an inhibitor of protein synthesis.
source: The effect on performance of the tasks was tested 20–24 hr after the injection of an inhibitor of protein synthesis.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol timing.

claim: Experiments with anisomycin injections were performed four times in monkey N and two times in monkey R.
source: We did experiments with anisomycin injections four times in monkey N and two times in monkey R.
evidence: This describes the number of experimental sessions conducted.

claim: Injections were spaced at least 7 days apart.
source: Injections were spaced at least 7 days apart.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol timing.

claim: The effect of muscimol on task performance was tested 20 min after the injection.
source: The effect of muscimol on task performance was tested 20 min after the injection to allow for some diffusion of the chemical in the brain tissue before resuming the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for control experiments.

claim: RTs less than 150 ms were considered to be predictive.
source: RTs less than 150 ms were considered to be predictive (Ohbayashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the criterion used for data analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: RTs less than 150 ms were chosen as a conservative cut-off for predictive responses as it is too fast for a simple reaction time to the visual cue.
source: RTs less than 150 ms were chosen as a conservative cut-off for predictive responses as it is too fast for a simple reaction time to the visual cue.
